subject: Medicine
summary: Hypoglycaemia is a low blood glucose state that can cause neuroglycopenic and autonomic symptoms. Prompt recognition, cause identification and glucose replacement are essential to prevent seizures and death.

sections.p: Hypoglycaemia is defined as a plasma glucose concentration low enough to cause symptoms, usually <3.0 mmol/L (55 mg/dL) in adults, with lower thresholds in children.
b: Measure capillary glucose when symptoms appear
Confirm with a second sample if possible

t.b: Does the patient have low glucose? A value <3.0 mmol/L confirms hypoglycaemia and guides immediate treatment.

sections.p: Severity is staged by symptoms and glucose level: mild (3.0‑3.9 mmol/L, autonomic signs), moderate (2.0‑2.9 mmol/L, neuroglycopenic signs), severe (<2.0 mmol/L, seizures or loss of consciousness).
b: Stage guides urgency of glucose replacement
Severe cases need IV dextrose immediately

sections.p: Identify the underlying mechanism: excess insulin, reduced intake, increased consumption, or impaired production.
b: Medication‑induced (insulin, sulfonylureas) – most common in diabetics
Fasting or poor feeding – common in infants and low‑resource settings
Severe infection (malaria, TB, HIV) – increases glucose utilization
Endocrine failure (adrenal, pituitary, hypothyroid) – reduces gluconeogenesis
Inborn errors of metabolism – rare but important in neonates

sections.p: Early autonomic signs (sweating, tremor, hunger) progress to neuroglycopenic features (confusion, lethargy, seizures, coma). In children, irritability and poor feeding are frequent.
b: Symptoms often worsen after a meal gap
Seizures indicate severe hypoglycaemia

sections.p: Beyond glucose, look for clues to cause and complications.
b: If a test is unavailable, treat empirically based on clinical picture and give glucose while searching for cause.

t.b: Is excess endogenous or exogenous insulin present? High insulin with high C‑peptide suggests endogenous overproduction; high insulin with low C‑peptide suggests exogenous insulin.
Is there ketosis? Low/absent ketones point to hyperinsulinaemic states; high ketones suggest fasting or adrenal insufficiency.

t.a: CBC, malaria smear, HIV test (if indicated)
t.b: Are infections contributing? Positive malaria or HIV can precipitate hypoglycaemia in low‑resource settings.
Is adrenal insufficiency present? Low cortisol supports Addisonian crisis.

sections.p: Uncontrolled hypoglycaemia can lead to irreversible brain injury, seizures, and death.
b: Seizure or loss of consciousness
Persistent glucose <2.0 mmol/L despite treatment
Acidosis or lactate rise

sections.p: Rapid glucose replacement, then treat the underlying cause.
b: IV 10 % dextrose bolus (if IV access) for severe cases – restores plasma glucose quickly
Oral glucose (tablet, gel, juice) for mild/moderate cases – safe and effective
Stop or adjust insulin/sulfonylurea dose – prevents recurrence
Treat infection (antimalarials, antibiotics, antiretrovirals) if present – removes consumptive cause
Give glucocorticoids for adrenal crisis – supports gluconeogenesis

sections.p: After acute correction, ensure stable glucose and address precipitating factors.
b: Educate patients on regular meals and glucose monitoring
Review medication regimens, especially insulin timing
Screen for endocrine disorders if recurrent
In children, ensure adequate feeding and monitor growth
Sepsis‑related encephalopathy – low glucose may be absent
Electrolyte disturbances (hyponatraemia) – cause similar confusion
Migraine aura – can produce visual changes but not sweating

sections.p: Laboratory values may be falsely normal.
b: Capillary glucose after recent oral glucose may be misleadingly high – repeat if doubt
Insulin assays can be affected by hemolysis – interpret with caution

whenToSeekHelp: Glucose remains <2.0 mmol/L after initial treatment

faq.a: Parasites consume glucose and release insulin‑like substances; antimalarial drugs (e.g., quinine) also stimulate insulin release.

faq.q: Can a patient feel normal with a glucose of 2.5 mmol/L?
faq.a: Rarely; most will have autonomic symptoms. If asymptomatic, verify the measurement and consider rapid repeat testing.

faq.q: Is oral glucose safe in a patient who is vomiting?
faq.a: No; use IV dextrose because vomiting prevents absorption and increases aspiration risk.

Interpret a low glucose with high insulin and low C‑peptide – what is the likely diagnosis and next step?

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic exam quickly differentiate true hypoglycaemia from mimics and point to the underlying mechanism, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: Onset: sudden vs gradual; relation to meals, fasting, or medication timing.
Recent intake: last carbohydrate, insulin, sulfonylurea, herbal remedies, alcohol.
Diabetes history: type, recent dose changes, missed meals, recent illness.
Pregnancy: gestational age, maternal diabetes, fetal movements.
Infection signs: fever, malaria, TB, HIV opportunistic infection.
Malnutrition or cachexia: recent weight loss, diet quality.
Family history of endocrine tumours or inborn errors of metabolism.

t.b: Observe level of consciousness, sweating, tremor; neuroglycopenic signs (confusion, seizures) indicate severe hypoglycaemia; cannot quantify glucose.
Check pulse, blood pressure; tachycardia may reflect adrenergic response; hypotension suggests adrenal insufficiency or sepsis; bedside cannot differentiate cause.
Palpate for hepatomegaly (possible glycogen storage disease) or masses; ascites may indicate liver failure; exam does not measure gluconeogenesis capacity.
Assess pupil size, reflexes, focal deficits; focal signs suggest intracranial pathology rather than pure hypoglycaemia; bedside cannot rule out seizures without EEG.
Look for hyperpigmentation (adrenal insufficiency), bruising (coagulopathy), or injection sites; cannot determine insulin level.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Select investigations that answer a specific clinical question; when a test is unavailable, treat empirically and seek alternative markers.
b: Capillary glucose (finger‑stick) – confirms symptomatic hypoglycaemia; <3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) with symptoms is diagnostic.
Serum glucose (laboratory) – validates capillary result; <3.9 mmol/L confirms hypoglycaemia, <3.0 mmol/L defines severe when neuroglycopenic signs present.
Serum insulin – high (>3 µU/mL or >18 pmol/L) with low glucose suggests hyperinsulinaemia.
C‑peptide – distinguishes endogenous (C‑peptide >0.6 ng/mL) from exogenous insulin excess.
Insulin/C‑peptide ratio – >1.0 supports endogenous hyperinsulinaemia (insulinoma, sulfonylurea).
Sulfonylurea screen – positive indicates drug‑induced hyperinsulinaemia; unavailable → rely on C‑peptide.
Blood ketones – low in hyperinsulinaemic states, high in starvation or adrenal failure.
Serum cortisol (8 am) – <3 µg/dL with low glucose points to adrenal insufficiency.
Lactate – elevated (>2 mmol/L) may indicate sepsis or tissue hypoxia; does not diagnose hypoglycaemia.
Full blood count, malaria rapid test, HIV rapid test – identify infection that raises glucose utilisation.

t.b: Re‑measure after 10–15 min post‑treatment; if still <3.9 mmol/L repeat dextrose.
High insulin with low C‑peptide → exogenous insulin overdose; high insulin with high C‑peptide → sulfonylurea or insulinoma.
Low cortisol with low glucose → primary adrenal insufficiency; treat with hydrocortisone after glucose correction.
Absent ketones in presence of low glucose suggests hyperinsulinaemia; presence supports starvation or adrenal failure.

sections.p: Classification combines glucose level, symptoms and need for assistance; it guides urgency of treatment and monitoring.
b: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia: capillary glucose <3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) with autonomic or neuroglycopenic symptoms.
Moderate hypoglycaemia: glucose <3.0 mmol/L (54 mg/dL) without seizures; oral glucose usually sufficient.
Severe hypoglycaemia: glucose <3.0 mmol/L (54 mg/dL) with seizures, loss of consciousness, or requiring assistance; IV dextrose or IM glucagon mandatory.
Refractory hypoglycaemia: glucose remains <3.0 mmol/L after two adequate dextrose boluses; search for insulin excess, adrenal failure, severe infection.
Persistent hypoglycaemia: repeated low readings over 24 h despite correction; indicates underlying endocrine or metabolic disorder.

sections.p: Several disorders mimic hypoglycaemia clinically or biochemically; a focused set of clues separates them.

t.b: Low glucose with high lactate, fever, tachycardia; ketones usually present; treat infection, give dextrose.
Low glucose, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, low cortisol; skin hyperpigmentation possible; give glucocorticoids after glucose.
Low glucose, high insulin, high C‑peptide; history of sulfonylurea exposure; give dextrose, consider activated charcoal.
Low glucose, high insulin, suppressed C‑peptide; often in diabetic patients with access to insulin; treat with dextrose, consider glucagon.

t.a: Inborn errors of metabolism (e.g., glycogen storage disease)
t.b: Neonatal/infant hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, elevated transaminases, fasting intolerance; enzyme assays or genetic testing required.
History of binge drinking, low glucose, normal/low insulin, elevated lactate; give glucose, monitor for withdrawal.

sections.p: A systematic approach ensures rapid glucose restoration, identification of cause, and prevention of recurrence while avoiding iatrogenic harm.
b: 1. Immediate safety: assess airway, breathing, circulation; place patient supine, give oxygen if needed.
2. Confirm hypoglycaemia with capillary glucose; if <3.9 mmol/L with symptoms, treat without delay.
3. Give rapid glucose: oral glucose (tablet, gel, juice) if conscious; if unconscious or no oral route, give IV 10 % dextrose 5 mL/kg bolus.
5. Re‑measure glucose after 10–15 min; repeat dextrose if still <3.9 mmol/L.
6. Once stable (≥3.9 mmol/L, symptoms resolved), start a maintenance infusion (e.g., 10 % dextrose 10 mL/kg/hr) to keep glucose >3.9 mmol/L.
7. Search for cause: review history, medications, infection, endocrine failure, malnutrition, organ dysfunction.
8. Escalate: call senior, consider ICU transfer if seizures persist, refractory hypoglycaemia, severe acidosis, or need for mechanical ventilation.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Understanding adverse effects and interactions prevents worsening hypoglycaemia and guides safe adjunct therapy.
b: Glucagon may cause nausea, vomiting, and transient tachycardia; if vomiting occurs, secure airway and consider repeat dextrose.
IV dextrose can precipitate hyperosmolarity; monitor serum sodium and avoid rapid large-volume boluses in renal failure.
Sulfonylureas increase insulin release; give glucagon or high‑dose dextrose and consider activated charcoal if ingestion <1 h.
Beta‑blockers mask autonomic signs and blunt gluconeogenesis; treat hypoglycaemia aggressively and avoid relying on symptoms.
Alcohol impairs hepatic gluconeogenesis; give dextrose and monitor for delayed hypoglycaemia after initial correction.

sections.p: Persistent or recurrent hypoglycaemia can cause irreversible brain injury; early recognition of complications triggers higher‑level care.
b: Neuroglycopenic seizures or loss of consciousness despite two dextrose boluses → ICU admission, continuous glucose infusion, EEG monitoring.
Severe metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.30, lactate > 4 mmol/L) indicates tissue hypoxia; treat with dextrose and consider bicarbonate per protocol.
Refractory hypoglycaemia (glucose <3.0 mmol/L after 30 min of adequate dextrose) suggests hyperinsulinaemia or adrenal insufficiency – request endocrine work‑up.
Cardiac arrhythmias in patients with underlying heart disease require cardiac monitoring and correction of electrolytes.
Persistent hypoglycaemia in pregnancy threatens fetal wellbeing; involve obstetrics, consider continuous maternal dextrose infusion, fetal monitoring.

sections.p: Co‑morbid conditions modify presentation, laboratory interpretation and therapeutic choices.
b: HIV/TB: opportunistic infections increase glucose utilisation; antiretrovirals (e.g., protease inhibitors) can cause insulin resistance – monitor closely.
Malnutrition: depleted glycogen stores limit endogenous glucose; give slower dextrose infusions to avoid re‑feeding syndrome.
Pregnancy: placental glucose transfer doubles fetal demand; treat mother aggressively and monitor fetal heart rate.
Diabetes on insulin or sulfonylureas: exogenous insulin causes low insulin/C‑peptide ratio; avoid giving additional insulin and use glucagon.
Herbal remedies (e.g., bitter melon) may potentiate insulin; inquire about traditional medicines.
Alcoholic liver disease: impaired gluconeogenesis; give dextrose slowly, watch for hypokalaemia.
Renal failure: reduced insulin clearance; lower insulin doses and avoid high‑dose dextrose boluses that may precipitate fluid overload.
Elderly: blunted autonomic response, polypharmacy; use lower‑volume dextrose and monitor for cardiac overload.

sections.p: Tailoring assessment and therapy to vulnerable populations improves outcomes in low‑resource settings.
b: Children (including neonates): use weight‑based dextrose bolus 2 mL/kg of 10 % dextrose; prefer oral glucose if alert; consider congenital hyperinsulinism – check insulin/C‑peptide.
Pregnancy: prioritize maternal glucose >3.9 mmol/L; avoid high‑dose glucagon if severe hypotension; involve obstetrics early.
Elderly: start with smaller dextrose volumes, monitor for fluid overload and cardiac ischemia; review all hypoglycaemia‑inducing drugs.
People with HIV: screen for opportunistic infections, drug‑drug interactions with antiretrovirals, and adrenal insufficiency.

Low‑resource settings: if glucometer unavailable, use urine dipstick for glucose, treat empirically with oral glucose or IV dextrose if IV line present, and send blood for laboratory confirmation when possible.

facts: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia: capillary glucose <3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL) with neuroglycopenic or autonomic signs.
Severe hypoglycaemia: glucose <3.0 mmol/L (54 mg/dL) or any neuroglycopenic symptom requiring assistance.
Moderate hypoglycaemia: glucose 3.0‑3.9 mmol/L (54‑70 mg/dL) with mild autonomic signs.
High serum insulin suggesting hyperinsulinaemia: >3 µU/mL (≈18 pmol/L) in the presence of low glucose.
Insulin/C‑peptide ratio >1.0 supports endogenous hyperinsulinaemia (insulinoma, sulfonylurea).
IV 10 % dextrose 5 mL/kg bolus raises plasma glucose by ~2‑3 mmol/L; repeat if still <3.9 mmol/L.
Re‑measure capillary glucose 10‑15 minutes after any glucose‑raising intervention.
Neonatal hypoglycaemia risk factors: maternal diabetes, prematurity, intra‑uterine growth restriction, prolonged fasting.
In low‑resource settings, malaria, severe infection and malnutrition are common precipitants.

vivas.q: Define severe hypoglycaemia and its clinical significance.
vivas.a: Glucose <3.0 mmol/L (54 mg/dL) or any neuroglycopenic symptom requiring assistance; it predicts risk of seizures, brain injury and death.

vivas.q: What is the first bedside step when a patient presents with altered mental status and suspected hypoglycaemia?
vivas.a: Check a capillary glucose immediately; if <3.9 mmol/L treat as hypoglycaemia while confirming with a second sample.

vivas.q: How do you differentiate exogenous insulin overdose from sulfonylurea toxicity using labs?
vivas.a: Exogenous insulin: high insulin, low C‑peptide; sulfonylurea: high insulin with high C‑peptide (ratio <1).

vivas.q: Why is rapid insulin bolus avoided in a patient with hypoglycaemia?
vivas.a: It would worsen low glucose and precipitate further neuroglycopenia; insulin should only be given after glucose is corrected.

vivas.q: Interpret: glucose 2.8 mmol/L, insulin 6 µU/mL, C‑peptide 0.4 ng/mL.
vivas.a: Suggests exogenous insulin excess (high insulin, low C‑peptide) – consider insulin overdose or factitious insulin.

vivas.q: List three common causes of hypoglycaemia in a non‑diabetic infant in a low‑resource hospital.
vivas.a: Prolonged fasting, severe infection (malaria, sepsis), inborn error of metabolism.

vivas.q: What bedside sign helps you recognise autonomic activation in hypoglycaemia?
vivas.a: Sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger – elicited by asking the patient and observing skin moisture and tremor.

vivas.q: What is the most likely syndrome in a newborn with omphalocele, macroglossia, organomegaly and hypoglycaemia?
Describe the stepwise management of a patient with hypoglycaemic seizure.
vivas.a: 1) Call for help, secure airway. 2) Give IV 10 % dextrose 5 mL/kg bolus. 3) Re‑measure glucose 10‑15 min. 4) Start continuous dextrose infusion (10 % at 10 mL/kg/hr). 5) Treat underlying cause.

vivas.q: Why must you re‑measure glucose after giving oral glucose gel?
vivas.a: To confirm adequate rise; oral absorption can be delayed or incomplete, especially in vomiting or altered consciousness.

vivas.q: What are red‑flag features that mandate urgent referral in an adult with persistent hypoglycaemia?
vivas.a: Seizures, loss of consciousness, glucose <3.0 mmol/L despite treatment, rising lactate, acidosis, or suspicion of insulinoma.

vivas.q: How does HIV infection modify the assessment of hypoglycaemia?
vivas.a: Opportunistic infections and antiretroviral drugs increase glucose utilization; co‑infection with TB or malaria may confound symptoms.

vivas.q: What is the recommended monitoring frequency after initial correction of severe hypoglycaemia?
vivas.a: Capillary glucose every 10‑15 minutes until stable, then hourly for the next 4‑6 hours.

vivas.q: Outline the key history questions for suspected hypoglycaemia.
vivas.a: Onset and timing of symptoms, recent meals, medication (insulin, sulfonylureas), alcohol, infections, pregnancy, previous episodes, family history of metabolic disease.

vivas.q: Why is a low glucose reading in a patient on high-dose steroids not misleading?
vivas.a: Steroids increase gluconeogenesis; a low reading despite steroids suggests a true pathological cause, not a lab artefact.

mcqs.q: A 4‑year‑old child with malaria presents with lethargy. Capillary glucose is 3.5 mmol/L. Which is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Observe and repeat glucose in 30 minutes
mcqs.e: Glucose <3.9 mmol/L with neuroglycopenic signs warrants IV dextrose bolus.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical autonomic symptom of hypoglycaemia?
Which condition is most strongly associated with recurrent neonatal hypoglycaemia and macroglossia?
mcqs.e: Beckwith‑Wiedemann presents with macroglossia, organomegaly and hypoglycaemia.

mcqs.q: A 70‑year‑old on metformin presents with confusion. Glucose is 3.8 mmol/L. Which factor most likely contributes to his low glucose?
mcqs.e: Renal impairment, alcohol, and exercise all increase metformin‑associated hypoglycaemia risk.

cases.v: A 2‑day‑old term infant, birth weight 4.2 kg, born to a mother with type 1 diabetes. At 12 hours of life the baby is jittery, sweaty and has a glucose of 2.6 mmol/L.

qs.q: What is the most likely cause of hypoglycaemia in this infant?

qs.a: Give buccal glucose gel or IV 10 % dextrose 5 mL/kg bolus; re‑measure glucose after 10‑15 min; start continuous dextrose infusion (10 % at 8‑10 mL/kg/hr).
Monitor glucose hourly for 24 h, check serum insulin and C‑peptide if persistent, screen for congenital hyperinsulinism if episodes recur.

cases.v: A 55‑year‑old farmer with known type 2 diabetes on sulfonylurea presents after a seizure. Capillary glucose is 1.9 mmol/L. He is unconscious, no IV line.

qs.q: After glucose is restored, what key laboratory test helps identify the cause?
qs.a: Serum C‑peptide; a low level with high insulin points to exogenous insulin, a high level suggests sulfonylurea.

qs.q: List two preventive measures for future episodes.
qs.a: Switch from sulfonylurea to a non‑hypoglycaemic agent; educate on regular meals and avoid alcohol.

mistakes: Using <3.0 mmol/L as the sole diagnostic cut‑off for symptomatic hypoglycaemia; WHO uses <3.9 mmol/L with symptoms.
Assuming insulin >5 µU/mL always indicates hyperinsulinaemia; the correct threshold is >3 µU/mL in low glucose.
Giving a 10 % dextrose bolus of 2 mL/kg; the recommended dose is 5 mL/kg.
Confusing endogenous and exogenous hyperinsulinaemia by not checking C‑peptide; low C‑peptide indicates exogenous insulin.
Repeating glucose measurement too soon (e.g., after 5 minutes); guideline is 10‑15 minutes.
Using glucagon in a patient with known adrenal insufficiency without giving steroids; adrenal crisis can worsen.
Failing to consider malaria or severe infection as precipitating factors in low‑resource settings.
